processing: Details are not documented. The name is recorded above the numbered scale of Georgian green tea grades; its use for black tea is unclear.
harvest_season: Made from the uppermost young leaves; a specific season is not recorded.
appearance_dry: Clean dark leaf with visible tips.
appearance_liquor: Clear amber, lighter than Indian or Ceylon black, as is general for Georgian tea.
appearance_wet: Small, even, coppery young leaves, as expected from upper-leaf picking.
taste_profile: Aromatic and soft rather than sharp, as with good Georgian black tea in general.

brewing.notes: Georgian tea extracts quickly and colours lightly. For a stronger cup use more leaf, 1.5 to 2 teaspoons per cup, not more time. Blending it with Indian or Ceylon tea hides its own taste.

vintage_note: Known as a Georgian trade grade, without documented vintages. A tea bearing the name today may have no connection to the old standard, so ask who made it and when.
description:
Georgian Bouquet, Buket Gruzii in Russian, was a top grade of Georgian tea. The name marks its place in the country's grading system more than any particular recipe.

Georgian green teas were numbered from No. 10, the lowest, up to No. 125. Buket Gruzii and Extra stood above the numbers. Whether and how the name was used for black tea is not clearly documented.

No reliable tasting notes are known, and it is not clear that this was a blend despite how the name sounds. If you find an old description, treat it as nostalgia until proven otherwise.

If you see it on sale now, ask who made it. For real Georgian character, a named modern small producer is a safer bet than an old grade name.
history: Georgian Bouquet is documented as part of the older Georgian grade system, at the top of both the black and the green ranges. Little is recorded about who introduced the name, or when.
